Content:
Recall that a sequence [MATH: a_n] for [MATH: n\geq 1] is a null sequence if it converges to zero:

[MATH: \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} a_n = 0]

Content:
Previously, we introduced the following formal definition of what this statement means:

Content:
> For any real [MATH: \varepsilon > 0] there exists a natural number [MATH: N] such that for every natural number [MATH: n \geq N,] if [MATH: n\geq N,] then [MATH: \left| a_n \right| \lt \varepsilon.]

In this lesson, we'll learn how to prove that a sequence is null.

Content:

sections.normalized_html:
Consider the following null sequence:

[MATH: a_n = \dfrac{2}{3n-7}, \qquad n\geq 1]

Let [MATH: \varepsilon > 0.] Find a natural number [MATH: N(\varepsilon)] such that for all [MATH: n\geq N,] we have [MATH: |a_n| < \varepsilon.]
sections.readable_text:
Consider the following null sequence:

[MATH: a_n = \dfrac{2}{3n-7}, \qquad n\geq 1]

Let [MATH: \varepsilon > 0.] Find a natural number [MATH: N(\varepsilon)] such that for all [MATH: n\geq N,] we have [MATH: |a_n| < \varepsilon.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, notice that [MATH: \dfrac{2}{3n-7} \gt 0] for any natural [MATH: n\geq 3.] So for [MATH: n\geq 3,] we have

[MATH: \left| \dfrac{2}{3n-7} \right| = \dfrac{2}{3n-7}.]

Now, we solve the inequality [MATH: |a_n| < \varepsilon] for [MATH: n\geq 3:]

[MATH: (2)/(3n − 7)|< ε; 2|< 3nε − 7ε; 2 + 7ε|< 3nε; (2)/(3ε) + (7)/(3)|< n; n|> (7)/(3) + (2)/(3ε)]

So, we let [MATH: N] be the smallest natural number such that [MATH: N > \dfrac 73 + \dfrac{2}{3\varepsilon}.]

Notice that, since [MATH: \dfrac{2}{3\varepsilon} > 0,] then [MATH: \dfrac 73 + \dfrac{2}{3\varepsilon} > \dfrac 73 = 2 \dfrac{1}{3}] and therefore [MATH: N \geq 3.]

Content:
Consider the following sequence once more:

Content:
[MATH: a_n = \dfrac{1}{n^2}, \qquad n \geq 1]

Content:
Let's now discuss how to construct a formal proof that [MATH: a_n] is null:

Content:
First, recall that

Content:
[MATH: \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} \left(\dfrac{1}{n^2}\right) = 0]

Content:
means (using formal notation) that

Content:
[MATH: \forall \varepsilon > 0, \: \exists N \in \mathbb{N}, \forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \: n \geq N \: \Rightarrow \: \left| \dfrac{1}{n^2} \right| \lt \varepsilon.]

Content:
We begin our proof by writing this in words:

Content:
> We need to show that for any real [MATH: \varepsilon > 0,] there exists a natural number [MATH: N] such that, for every natural number [MATH: n \geq N,] we have
> [MATH: \left| \dfrac{1}{n^2} \right| \lt \varepsilon.]

Content:
Earlier in the lesson, we showed that for any [MATH: \varepsilon > 0,] if we let [MATH: N] be the smallest natural number such that

Content:
[MATH: N > \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon}}]

Content:
then [MATH: |a_n| < \varepsilon] for all [MATH: n\geq N.]

Content:
Using this result, we continue the proof:

Content:
> Suppose [MATH: \varepsilon > 0.] Let's choose some natural number [MATH: N > \dfrac{1}{\sqrt\varepsilon}.]

Content:
With that in mind, we show that [MATH: \varepsilon] is an upper bound of [MATH: |a_n|] for [MATH: n\geq N{:}]

Content:
> Then, for any natural number [MATH: n \geq N,] we have
> [MATH: |(1)/(n^{2})||= (1)/(n^{2}); < (1)/((1/sqrt(ε))^{2}); = (1)/(1/ε); = ε]

Content:
Finally, we make the conclusion:

Content:
> Therefore, according to the definition, [MATH: \displaystyle \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} \left(\dfrac{1}{n^2}\right) = 0.]

Content:
Now that we've figured out all the details, let's write down our formal proof.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Recall that a sequence [MATH: a_n] for [MATH: n\geq 1] is a null sequence if it converges to zero:

Content:
[MATH: \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} a_n = 0]

Content:
Previously, we introduced the following formal definition of what this statement means:

Content:
> For any real [MATH: \varepsilon > 0] there exists a natural number [MATH: N] such that for every natural number [MATH: n \geq N,] if [MATH: n\geq N,] then [MATH: \left| a_n \right| \lt \varepsilon.]

Content:
This concept is illustrated in the picture below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f86d3ec2479b5b77eda405cc3e09280b]

Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to prove that a sequence is null.

Content:
Constructing a proof that a sequence is null mostly boils down to finding a suitable [MATH: N(\varepsilon)] that satisfies the definition. So, let's get some practice with that first.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Finding a Suitable Value of N

Content:
Consider the following null sequence:

Content:
[MATH: a_n = \dfrac{1}{n^2}, \qquad n \geq 1]

Content:
Given that [MATH: \varepsilon > 0,] let's find a natural number [MATH: N(\varepsilon)] such that for all [MATH: n \geq N,] we have

Content:
[MATH: |a_n| < \varepsilon.]

Content:
First, notice that our sequence is positive for any natural [MATH: n \geq 1.] With that in mind, we have

Content:
[MATH: |a_n| = \left| \dfrac{1}{n^2} \right| = \dfrac{1}{n^2}.]

Content:
Now, we solve the inequality [MATH: |a_n| < \varepsilon] for [MATH: n{:}]

Content:
[MATH: (1)/(n^{2})|< ε; 1|< εn^{2}; (1)/(ε)|< n^{2}; (1)/(sqrt(ε))|< n; n|> (1)/(sqrt(ε))]

Content:
So, we let [MATH: N] be the smallest natural number such that

Content:
[MATH: N > \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon}}.]

Content:
And that's it! Given any [MATH: \varepsilon > 0,] no matter how small, [MATH: |a_n|] is guaranteed to be smaller than [MATH: \varepsilon] provided that [MATH: n\geq N,] where [MATH: N] is the smallest natural number greater than [MATH: \dfrac{1}{\sqrt\varepsilon}.]

---

Explanation:
First, notice that [MATH: \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \gt 0] for any natural [MATH: n \geq 1.] With that in mind, we have

Now, we solve the inequality [MATH: |a_n| < \varepsilon] for [MATH: n]:

[MATH: (1)/(sqrt(n))|< ε; 1|< εsqrt(n); 1|< nε^{2}; (1)/(ε^{2})|< n; n|> (1)/(ε^{2})]

So, we let [MATH: N] be the smallest natural number such that
[MATH: N > \dfrac{1}{\varepsilon^2}.]

First, notice that [MATH: \dfrac{2}{3n-7} \gt 0] for any natural [MATH: n\geq 3.] So for [MATH: n\geq 3,] we have

[MATH: N > \dfrac 73 + \dfrac{2}{3\varepsilon}.]

Notice that, since [MATH: \dfrac{2}{3\varepsilon} > 0,] then [MATH: \dfrac 73 + \dfrac{2}{3\varepsilon} > \dfrac 73 = 2 \dfrac{1}{3}] and therefore [MATH: N \geq 3.]
